newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.Africa's new CPI weighting - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.Africa's new CPI weighting - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

The conclusion of the Boskin special commission of investigation into the reliability of U.S. economic statistics that the official U.S. inflation figures were badly overstated has been rejected by many as being over-zealous and deeply flawed.
Broadly, Boskin estimated that the CPI was overstated by 1.1 percentage points, so instead of the official three percent U.S. inflation rate the figure should be just under two percent.

The implications of this for the U.S. economy are profound for it implies an understatement of real performance of the American economy. And index linked public pensions and tax thresholds and the like should have a lower rate of increase in the future, leading to increased budgetary revenues and lower expenditures.
An easy way of reducing chronic budgetary deficits would be in prospect but, of course, all vested interests have been alerted and a fierce challenge to the conclusions has been aroused.

Boskin's assessment is based on three arguments. Firstly, some increased prices could reflect an improvement in quality of goods and services and, therefore, should not be fully inflationary - contributing 0.6 percent points. Secondly, consumers change their spending as relative prices change - the substitution of pears for apples as pears become relatively cheaper - this contributes 0.4 percent points. And thirdly, the movement towards discount shops away from traditional outlets contributes the other 0.1 percent point.

The improvement in quality argument has been criticised for being exaggerated, for, while acknowledging general quality improvements, the developments have been much slower than assumed by Boskin and the Bureau of Labour Statistics responsible for the CPI figures does make efforts to account for quality improvements. It has also been noted that the quality of some goods and services has worsened with U.S. education given as an example.

As far as the substitution factor is concerned there is a counter argument of some validity that consumers may have a definite preference and there would be some loss of utility in having to purchase the other product, but how is this to be dealt with in the compilation of the figures?

Statistical services are always professionally aware of these problems and do their best to overcome them through a close monitoring of prices of comparable products, periodic updating of reporting distribution outlets, and periodic surveys of household consumption patterns.
